title: CoT is Not the Chain of Truth: An Empirical Internal Analysis of Reasoning LLMs for Fake News Generation
shortTitle: CoT is Not the Chain of Truth
tldr: We study unsafe content in generated reasoning traces, localize safety-related layers and attention heads with Jacobian spectral analysis, and evaluate targeted safety interventions on fake-news generation and HarmBench.
abstract: From generating headlines to fabricating news, Large Language Models (LLMs) are typically assessed by their final outputs, under the safety assumption that a refusal response signifies safe reasoning throughout the entire process. Challenging this assumption, our study reveals that during fake news generation, even when a model rejects a harmful request, its Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning may still internally contain and propagate unsafe narratives. To analyze this phenomenon, we introduce a unified safety-analysis framework that systematically deconstructs CoT generation across model layers and evaluates the role of individual attention heads through Jacobian-based spectral metrics. Within this framework, we introduce three interpretable measures—stability, geometry, and energy—to quantify how specific attention heads respond to or embed deceptive reasoning patterns. Extensive experiments on multiple reasoning-oriented LLMs show that the generation risk rises significantly when the thinking mode is activated, where the critical routing decisions are concentrated in only a few contiguous mid-depth layers.

methodOverview: We build a coarse-to-fine pipeline: (1) generate and annotate CoT traces under direct/indirect fake-news prompts; (2) localize safety-critical mid-depth layers; (3) attribute divergence to attention heads using Jacobian-based stability (B1), geometry (B2), and energy (B3) metrics; (4) validate with perturbation analysis and critical-head mitigation.
contributions: Unsafe and Potential Unsafe traces together reach about 78-81% in the reported fake-news generation settings, including cases where the final answer refuses.
A layer-to-head framework that localizes safety-critical routing in contiguous mid-depth windows.
Three Jacobian spectral metrics, B1-B3, for interpretable head-level attribution of unsafe reasoning.
Generalization on HarmBench and critical-head fine-tuning that updates 0.64%-1.95% of parameters and raises CoT safety by +67.1 on news and +55.0 on HarmBench on average.
mainResults: Thinking mode raises the share of Unsafe and Potential Unsafe traces to about 78-81% across Llama3-8B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-8B.
Safe and unsafe trajectories diverge in contiguous mid-depth layer windows for both direct and indirect prompting.
Unsafe routing concentrates in a small subset of attention heads with distinct B1, B2, and B3 spectral signatures.
Critical-head fine-tuning improves CoT safety by +67.1 on news and +55.0 on HarmBench on average.
priorWorkDiff: The analysis links annotated reasoning traces to model layers and individual attention heads. Jacobian-based measurements characterize stability, geometry, and spectral energy, and perturbation experiments and targeted updates evaluate the identified components.

generalizationSummary: Beyond fake-news generation, we evaluate HarmBench jailbreak tasks on Flan-UL2 and DeepSeek-R1-70B. Safe vs. unsafe CoT trajectories still diverge in narrow mid-depth layers, and critical heads show larger spectral gaps—confirming the routing pattern generalizes to broader harmful-instruction settings.
correlationSummary: B1–B3 correlate strongly with safety-relevant routing across all three models.

introText: The study annotates generated reasoning traces as Safe, Potential Unsafe, or Unsafe and records final-answer behavior. Experiments examine direct and indirect fake-news generation prompts, multiple stylistic settings, and the effects of thinking mode. This process-level view supports analysis of the relationship between trace content, final-answer refusal, and internal model components.

faqs.q: What does reasoning-trace safety evaluation measure?
faqs.a: It measures the safety of content produced during a model's reasoning process. This study annotates generated traces as Safe, Potential Unsafe, or Unsafe and examines their relationship with final-answer behavior.

faqs.q: How does final-answer refusal relate to reasoning-trace safety?
faqs.a: The experiments identify unsafe content in reasoning traces whose final answers are refusals. Trace annotations, generation statistics, and internal model analysis characterize this relationship.

faqs.q: How are safety-related layers and attention heads identified?
faqs.a: The workflow first examines behavior across model layers and then measures individual attention heads within the localized layer windows. Jacobian spectral metrics, perturbation experiments, and targeted updates support the analysis.

faqs.q: What do the Jacobian spectral metrics characterize?
faqs.a: The three metrics characterize stability under perturbation, the geometry of information flow, and spectral energy concentration. They provide complementary measurements for attention-head analysis.

faqs.q: Which tasks are included in the evaluation?
faqs.a: The paper studies fake-news generation and reports additional evaluation on HarmBench jailbreak tasks. The HarmBench experiments include Flan-UL2 and DeepSeek-R1-70B.

faqs.q: Which analysis components are available in the repository?
faqs.a: The repository contains generation, annotation, layer-analysis, and attention-head-analysis entry points in CoT_Generation, CoT_Annotation, and CoT_Analysis. The project resources link directly to these components.

researchQuestion: How can reasoning-trace safety be evaluated and localized inside language models?
researchContext: Reasoning-model safety connects the content of generated reasoning traces with the internal computations that produce them. CoT is Not the Chain of Truth studies unsafe reasoning traces whose final answers are refusals and develops a layer-to-head workflow for analyzing this behavior.

The study connects process-level safety evaluation, mechanistic interpretability, and targeted safety intervention. It combines trace annotation with Jacobian-based measurements of stability, geometry, and spectral energy, and evaluates the identified components through perturbation experiments and targeted updates.

researchNote.author: Chunlin Gong
researchNote.lead: Generated reasoning traces provide a detailed record for studying language-model safety. They support questions about the content produced during reasoning, the internal components associated with that content, and interventions that improve safety. These questions connect evaluation, mechanistic interpretability, and model control.

sections.title: Evaluating reasoning traces
paragraphs: A process-level evaluation records the prompt, the generated reasoning trace, and the final answer. Trace annotations characterize the content produced during reasoning, while final-answer labels capture the model's response to the request. Studying these observations together reveals how safety behavior develops through generation.

CoT is Not the Chain of Truth examines this relationship in fake-news generation, including traces containing unsafe content whose final answers are refusals. Its analysis combines trace annotation with measurements of internal model behavior. The paper also reports evaluation on HarmBench jailbreak tasks.

sections.title: Localizing safety-related computation
paragraphs: Internal analysis connects observed generation behavior with model components. Layer-level measurements identify relevant depth intervals, and attention-head analysis examines components within those intervals. Jacobian-based measurements characterize sensitivity, geometry, and spectral energy.

This workflow gives researchers a route from an annotated trace to a concrete set of components for further study. Perturbation experiments and targeted updates connect these measurements with observed changes in model behavior.

sections.title: Connecting evaluation, refusal, and intervention
paragraphs: SafeChain studies the safety of long-reasoning models through evaluation, decoding strategies, and CoT-style safety training. Where Do Reasoning Models Refuse? examines refusal decisions within reasoning traces and internal representations. Chain-of-Thought Hijacking investigates extended reasoning, refusal robustness, and internal safety signals.

These research directions motivate complementary questions about trace content, refusal decisions, model mechanisms, and safety interventions. CoT is Not the Chain of Truth contributes a layer-to-head analysis workflow using Jacobian spectral measurements and evaluates targeted interventions in the reported experimental settings.

sections.title: Working with the analysis workflow
paragraphs: The public repository organizes the workflow into generation, annotation, and layer/head analysis. Researchers can start with the prompt and data-format documentation, inspect the annotation entry points, and follow the analysis scripts to understand the reported measurements.
The project page collects the framework, experiments, figures, and official ICML 2026 citation. Its resource links connect each part of the workflow to the corresponding repository directory.
